name: Hair-growth inhibitor lotion

card.summary: Lotions that slow hair regrowth: one Rx ingredient (eflornithine) has trial data, OTC versions have little.
card.note: Effect reverses after stopping; OTC formulations vary and are unstudied here.

quick.overview:
These lotions aim to slow how fast unwanted hair comes back. The prescription version, eflornithine cream, is used for facial hair in women and has clinical data behind it.

Over-the-counter retardant lotions are a loose category with varied ingredients, and no trials of them were found.
quick.mechanism: Eflornithine blocks an enzyme (ornithine decarboxylase) in the follicle, which slows hair growth rather than removing hair.
quick.risks: Acne, stinging, itching and rash are reported with eflornithine. Hair regrows to baseline within about eight weeks of stopping.

lead: Hair-growth inhibitor lotions are topical products used to slow how quickly unwanted facial or body hair comes back after shaving, waxing or plucking. People use them to keep skin smoother for longer between hair-removal sessions, to cut down on shadow and stubble, and to reduce the visible upkeep of a clean-shaven or hair-free look. The term covers one prescription cream and a range of over-the-counter lotions sold as hair retardants or inhibitors.

The best-documented active ingredient is eflornithine, sold as a prescription facial cream (brand names Vaniqa and Follinil) for women with excess facial hair. It blocks an enzyme in the hair follicle called ornithine decarboxylase, which slows the growth of the hair rather than removing it.[1][3] Wikipedia reports that in clinical studies 81 percent of women showed improvement after twelve months, that results began to appear around eight weeks, and that hair returned to baseline within about eight weeks of stopping.[1] Eflornithine has also been used as a reference hair-growth inhibitor in laboratory work on human hair follicles.[2]

Randomized split-face trials have tested eflornithine cream alone and together with laser hair removal, and patient-reported studies have measured how much it reduces the bother of facial hair.[5][6][7] Over-the-counter retardant lotions are a looser category. Their ingredients differ by brand, and Wikipedia's hair-removal article lists them among non-prescription methods sold with limited published clinical data.[3]

chain: Lotion is applied to skin after shaving or waxing
Follicle activity is slowed (eflornithine blocks ornithine decarboxylase)
Hair regrows more slowly, so skin stays smooth longer
angle.text: Users apply the product to areas such as the face, lip or body after hair removal so the hair reappears more slowly and the smooth look lasts longer between sessions. The prescription cream is described as reducing the psychological burden of facial hair for women who have it [1]. The effect lasts only while the product is used.

paras: The idea behind a hair-growth inhibitor is different from hair removal. Shaving, waxing, plucking and depilatory creams take hair off at or below the skin, with results lasting hours to weeks, and depilatories dissolve hair chemically by breaking the disulfide bonds that give it strength.[3] An inhibitor is applied afterwards to the same skin and aims to slow how fast the next hair grows in, so the smooth look lasts longer and there is less visible stubble.[3]

Facial hair in women is the best-studied setting. Wikipedia describes hirsutism as male-pattern hair growth in women that affects between 5 and 15 percent of women, most often linked to polycystic ovary syndrome, and notes that facial-hair-related stigma often leads people to avoid social situations.[4] Cosmetic hair removal can be used alone or alongside drug therapy.[4]

Eflornithine acts as a suicide inhibitor of ornithine decarboxylase, an enzyme needed for cell growth in the hair follicle. It binds the enzyme irreversibly, and Wikipedia notes that two molecules are required for full inhibition because the enzyme has two active sites.[1] Hair cells use the enzyme to make putrescine, which they need to stabilise their DNA, so hair growth gradually decreases with continued use and returns to normal if use stops.[3] It is described as the only prescription topical treatment that slows facial hair growth.[1] Normal hair removal such as shaving or depilation can continue alongside treatment.[3]

Wikipedia describes topical absorption as negligible, and lists the more serious adverse effects, such as blood-cell changes and seizures, under the intravenous form used for sleeping sickness.[1] Acne is the most commonly reported side effect, at 7 to 14 percent. Ingrown-hair skin reactions, stinging, burning or tingling, dryness, itching, redness and rash have also been reported.[1] Safety in pregnancy is described as unclear, with limited topical data showing no clear harm.[1]

Non-prescription products sold as hair retardants, inhibitors or growth reducers are typically used after shaving or waxing. Their active ingredients vary by brand. Wikipedia's hair-removal article groups these preparations among "doubtful methods" for which published clinical proof of the claimed effect is lacking.[3] No randomized trial of a specific over-the-counter retardant lotion was located.
Because ingredients differ between brands, the category is defined by what the products are sold to do rather than by one shared mechanism as with eflornithine.[3]

sections.h: Use with laser and light-based removal
paras: Several trials examined eflornithine as an add-on to laser hair removal, which Wikipedia reports became widespread in the 1990s and has been FDA-approved since 1997.[3] In a 2006 randomized trial, 54 women had eflornithine on one side of the face and a vehicle cream on the other for 34 weeks, with both sides getting laser sessions at weeks 2 and 10. The eflornithine side showed significant hair reduction from weeks 6 through 22, no significant difference remained at week 34 on blinded evaluator comparison, and patients' own grading showed a persistent difference through week 34. The authors concluded that eflornithine can be safely combined with laser and that patients preferred the combination.[5]

A 2007 randomized, double-blind, right-left study of 31 evaluable women treated the upper lip with laser every four weeks for up to six sessions plus either eflornithine or placebo cream twice daily. Complete or near-complete hair removal occurred at 93.5 percent of eflornithine sites against 67.9 percent of placebo sites, and the authors reported that the combination gave faster and more complete reduction over up to six months, although they did not determine how long the benefit lasted afterwards.[6] A 2016 split-face trial in the Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology and later trials from Pakistan and in 2025 have continued to compare eflornithine plus intense pulsed light with light-based treatment alone.[9][10][11]
The Drug and Therapeutics Bulletin published an appraisal of the question in 2007.[12]

A 2007 analysis in the International Journal of Dermatology drew on two randomized trials of eflornithine 13.9 percent cream. Women rated facial hair as highly bothersome, with mean overall bother of 89 percent and discomfort in social situations above 80 percent for nearly all items, and treatment significantly reduced bother on all six measures, with effect sizes from 0.46 to 1.62. The authors concluded that eflornithine was effective by patients' own reports.[7]

Merrell Dow Research Institute developed eflornithine in the late 1970s as a cancer treatment. It did not work against malignancies, but researchers observed that it strongly reduced hair growth, and it was also found to treat African sleeping sickness. It was registered for that use on 28 November 1990.[1] Aventis stopped producing it in 1995 because it was unprofitable, and a 2001 partnership between Aventis and the World Health Organization restored supply.[1] The topical cream later received marketing approval from the US FDA and the European Commission for facial hair in women.[1]

Antiandrogen medicines such as spironolactone and finasteride are used by prescribers for unwanted hair in women. Wikipedia says they can slow facial hair and prevent new hair, but have little effect on existing facial hair, and that antiandrogens other than the 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors are contraindicated in men because of feminising side effects.[3] A 2015 Cochrane review of 157 randomized studies with about 10,550 women found flutamide and spironolactone appeared effective and reasonably safe, though with low to very low quality evidence, and oral contraceptives seemed helpful for mild hirsutism; it reviewed oral and topical treatments other than laser or light therapy alone.[8] These are a different category from topical lotions.

Methods that remove or destroy follicles are separate from inhibitors. Wikipedia lists electrolysis, in US practice since 1875, as the only permanent method the FDA recognises, while laser and intense pulsed light can give long-term reduction after several sessions.[3]

No studies found for over-the-counter hair-growth inhibitor lotions. For prescription eflornithine, clinical studies reported improvement in 81 percent of women after twelve months, with hair regrowth to baseline after stopping,[1] and the randomized trials above studied it with laser hair removal and for patient-reported bother.[5][6][7] A laboratory study of human hair follicles in culture used eflornithine as a clinically used topical hair-growth inhibitor and found that it induced premature entry into the regression phase (catagen).[2]

timeline.event: Electrolysis begins to be practised in the US, later the only method the FDA recognises as permanent.[3]
Merrell Dow Research Institute develops eflornithine as a cancer drug and observes reduced hair growth.[1]
Eflornithine is registered for gambiense sleeping sickness on 28 November.[1]
Aventis stops producing eflornithine as unprofitable.[1]
Laser hair removal receives FDA approval.[3]
Aventis and the WHO partner to restore eflornithine supply for sleeping sickness.[1]
Eflornithine cream (Vaniqa) approved for facial hair in women by the US FDA and the European Commission.[1]
Randomized trial of eflornithine plus laser in 54 women is published in Dermatologic Surgery.[5]
A laser plus eflornithine upper-lip study and an analysis of patient-reported bother are published.[6][7]
Cochrane review of 157 studies of hirsutism interventions is published.[8]
Split-face trial tests adjuvant eflornithine to maintain intense-pulsed-light hair reduction.[9]
